stances.claim: FVR's relationship with the judiciary -- a topic less written about than his workaholism, CSW/UST demands, 'bibingka' approach, democratic reform, doable agenda, and 'Philippines 2000' vision -- is best illustrated by two cases that show his deep respect for the Supreme Court and the rule of law.

Alex David v. Comelec (April 8, 1997) -- which CJ had the honor of writing -- unanimously denied the petition to extend barangay-official terms from three to five years, in strongly worded language ('completely devoid of merit'; 'subtle but nonetheless self-serving propositions to lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed'), despite Palace media-buzz preferences for postponement and the OSG's siding with petitioners against its own Comelec client.

Despite the decision's strong language, FVR did not balk, complain, or hint regret at CJ's authorship; he simply asked everyone, including dissenters, to obey because the Court had spoken -- modeling the rule-of-law-comes-first temperament.

Defensor-Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997), much more controversial than the first, held by an 8-5 vote (Davide ponencia) that RA 6735 was inadequate for people's initiative; CJ dissented along with Melo, Puno, Mendoza, and Francisco on the novel-and-unprecedented 'insufficient or inadequate law' theory -- 'a law is either constitutional or unconstitutional but never inadequate or insufficient.'

The MR vote came out 6-6 -- failing the required seven votes for reversal -- and was denied with finality. Critically, FVR never asked his nine appointees (who outnumbered the six others) to vote one way or the other, even though a unified bloc could have unlocked his 1998 reelection via people's initiative; he respected the Court's independence to decide freely.

notable_anecdotes: FVR's hallmark catalogue -- workaholic, CSW (completed staff work), UST (units of time), 'bibingka' metaphor, abhorrence of autocratic shortcuts, doable legislative agenda, 'Philippines 2000' -- compressed into a single sentence as the column's biographical thumbnail.

The Alex David ponencia's four-clause refutation -- 'The Constitution and the laws do not support them. Extant jurisprudence militates against them. Reason and common sense reject them. Equity and morality abhor them' -- a quintessentially CJ-style cascading-clause refusal.

OSG-siding-with-petitioners detail -- 'instead of defending its client, the respondent Comelec -- the Office of the Solicitor General (the government's counsel) opted to side with the petitioners' -- quietly documenting Palace influence on the government's own legal arm.

The Defensor-Santiago dissenter line-up -- Melo, Puno, Mendoza, Francisco, and CJ -- preserved as a doctrinal memoir, with the explicit grievance that 'a law is either constitutional or unconstitutional but never inadequate or insufficient.'

The counterfactual close -- 'if all the appointees of FVR lined up their votes solidly, the respondents could have succeeded in their advocacy to amend the Constitution via a people's initiative and enabled FVR to run for and win reelection in 1998' -- making FVR's non-intervention the heart of the column's moral.

The biographical aside -- that CJ himself was the ponente in Alex David and a dissenter in Defensor-Santiago -- making the entire column a first-person memoir of two SC moments where FVR's restraint was tested.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban fills a void in the FVR tributes -- beyond Fidel V. Ramos's legendary workaholism, demand for CSW (completed staff work) and UST (units of time), 'bibingka' approach, passion for democratic reform matched by his abhorrence of autocratic shortcuts, doable legislative agenda, and 'Philippines 2000' vision -- by recounting how FVR greatly respected the Supreme Court and unflinchingly followed the rule of law, through two cases. In Alex David v. Comelec (April 8, 1997), which CJ had the honor of writing, the Court unanimously denied a petition to extend barangay-official terms from three to five years and cancel the May 12, 1997 barangay elections -- despite media buzz that FVR wanted the postponement, and despite the OSG siding with petitioners against its own Comelec client. The ponencia's language was strong: 'The Constitution and the laws do not support them. Extant jurisprudence militates against them. Reason and common sense reject them. Equity and morality abhor them. They are subtle but nonetheless self-serving propositions to lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed.' Yet FVR did not balk or complain -- he asked everyone, including dissenters, to obey, and never hinted regret at CJ's authorship. In the more controversial Defensor-Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997), the Court held 8-5 -- Davide ponencia joined by CJ Narvasa, JJ Regalado, Romero, Bellosillo, Kapunan, Hermosisima, and Torres against dissenters Melo, Puno, Mendoza, Francisco, and CJ himself -- that RA 6735 was inadequate for people's initiative. The dissenters attacked the novel 'insufficient or inadequate law' theory ('a law is either constitutional or unconstitutional but never inadequate or insufficient'). The MR split 6-6, failing the seven votes needed to reverse, and was denied with finality. Crucially, FVR never asked his nine appointees (who outnumbered the six others) to vote one way or the other -- even though a unified bloc could have unlocked his 1998 reelection via people's initiative. 'Indeed, he respected the independence and dignity of the Court and its members to decide freely in accordance with its/their constitutional mandate.'
